cards.title: Hyperion

source.name: Hesiod, Theogony; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 134 (Hyperion among the Titans); Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.192 (the Sun called 'Hyperione natus,' son of Hyperion).

cards.summary_basic: Hyperion was a Titan of light, often identified with the sun itself, and a byword for radiant male beauty. When Hamlet compares his father to 'Hyperion' and his uncle Claudius to 'a satyr' (a coarse, goatish, lustful woodland creature), he is setting a shining sun-god against a beast.
cards.detail_scholar: In Hesiod's Theogony Hyperion is one of the Titans, father of Helios (the Sun), Selene (the Moon), and Eos (the Dawn); by Shakespeare's day the name was frequently used for the sun-god directly. The contrast with the satyr is total: divine versus bestial, light versus appetite. Shakespeare returns to Hyperion as an image of beauty and kingship elsewhere (e.g. Troilus and Cressida 4.5).

cards.title: Niobe

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.146–312 (Golding's 1567 English translation was Shakespeare's likely source).

cards.summary_basic: Niobe was a queen of Thebes who boasted that her fourteen children made her greater than the goddess Leto, who had only two. In revenge those two — Apollo and Diana — killed all of Niobe's children with arrows. Niobe wept without stopping until the gods turned her to stone, and even the stone kept weeping. She is the classical byword for inconsolable grief.
cards.detail_scholar: Hamlet says his mother followed his father's body 'Like Niobe, all tears' — and then, within a month, remarried. The allusion measures the gap between performed grief and real constancy: Niobe's mourning was eternal and turned her to stone; Gertrude's lasted weeks. Ovid's Niobe was a standard school text in Tudor grammar schools.

cards.title: The Nemean lion (Hercules' first labour)

source.name: Apollodorus, Library; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.1 (the lion of Nemea, slain as the first of the twelve labours); Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.182–210 (Hercules recounts his labours).

cards.summary_basic: The Nemean lion was a monstrous beast whose hide no weapon could pierce. Strangling it was the first of the twelve labours of Hercules, the greatest hero-strongman of Greek myth. To invoke 'the Nemean lion's nerve [sinew]' is to invoke superhuman strength and fearlessness.
cards.detail_scholar: Hamlet, breaking from his friends to follow the Ghost, says his fate makes each artery 'as hardy as the Nemean lion's nerve.' The allusion casts his resolve in heroic, almost reckless terms — and Hercules is a figure Hamlet measures himself against and finds himself unlike ('no more like my father / Than I to Hercules').

cards.title: Lethe, river of forgetfulness

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 6.703–715 (the souls drink of Lethe to forget); Ovid, Metamorphoses 11.602–604 (Lethe by the cave of Sleep).

cards.summary_basic: Lethe was one of the rivers of the classical underworld; the spirits of the dead drank from it to forget their earthly lives. 'Lethe wharf' means the bank or shore of oblivion. When the Ghost tells Hamlet that a man would have to be duller than the weeds rotting 'on Lethe wharf' not to be stirred by this story, he is saying: only the utterly forgetful and lifeless could fail to act.
cards.detail_scholar: The image fuses forgetting and death — appropriate to a Ghost demanding to be 'remembered.' Memory versus forgetting runs through the whole play (the Ghost's parting command is 'remember me'; Hamlet vows to wipe all 'trivial fond records' from the 'table of his memory').

cards.title: Hecuba, Queen of Troy

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses; Euripides
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.404–575; Euripides, Hecuba and Trojan Women (the archetype of maternal grief).

cards.summary_basic: Hecuba was the queen of Troy who watched her husband King Priam and most of her children killed when the Greeks sacked the city. She became the ancient world's byword for absolute grief. When the Player weeps real tears over Hecuba, Hamlet is shamed that an actor can feel more for a legend than Hamlet feels for his own murdered father — 'What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba, / That he should weep for her?'
cards.detail_scholar: The Player's speech is built from the matter of Virgil's Aeneid 2 and the Troy legend. Hecuba's grief — and her later transformation into a howling dog — was a school commonplace; Shakespeare uses it to launch Hamlet's self-accusing soliloquy 'O what a rogue and peasant slave am I.'

cards.title: The fall of Troy: Pyrrhus and Priam

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 2.506–558 (Pyrrhus/Neoptolemus kills the aged King Priam at the altar during the sack of Troy).

cards.summary_basic: When Troy fell, the Greek warrior Pyrrhus (son of Achilles) butchered the old, defenceless King Priam in front of his family. The Player's set-piece about 'the rugged Pyrrhus' and the 'Hyrcanian beast' (a tiger from a region by the Caspian, a byword for savagery) retells this slaughter. It shadows the play's own theme: a son's revenge, an old king murdered.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare's source is the Aeneas-to-Dido narration in Aeneid 2, possibly via a lost play or Marlowe & Nashe's Dido. The Pyrrhus/Priam parallel quietly mirrors and inverts Hamlet's situation — Pyrrhus is the avenging son who does not hesitate.

cards.title: Hercules and his labours

source.name: Apollodorus, Library; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.8–2.7; Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.1–272 (the twelve labours and death of Hercules).

cards.summary_basic: Hercules (Greek Herakles) was the strongest hero of classical myth, famous for completing twelve near-impossible 'labours.' He stands for sheer, decisive strength. Hamlet measures himself against Hercules and finds himself wanting — 'no more like my father / Than I to Hercules' — and later mutters that even Hercules cannot stop the world's pettiness ('Let Hercules himself do what he may').
cards.detail_scholar: The phrase 'Hercules and his load too' (2.2) also glances at the Globe theatre's own sign, said to show Hercules bearing the globe — an in-joke about the rival boy-companies stealing the adult players' audience.

cards.title: Roscius, the great Roman actor

source.name: Cicero
source.citation: Quintus Roscius Gallus (d. 62 BCE), the most celebrated comic actor of Rome; Cicero, Pro Q. Roscio Comoedo and De Oratore 1.130.

cards.summary_basic: Roscius was the most famous actor of ancient Rome — so admired that his name became shorthand for 'a superb performer.' When Polonius announces the players, Hamlet mockingly caps him: 'When Roscius was an actor in Rome…' — teasing the old man for delivering stale news as if it were fresh.

cards.title: Fortune and her wheel

source.name: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy
source.citation: Boethius, Consolatio Philosophiae II, prose 1–2 (Fortune turning her wheel) — the central late-antique/medieval image of fate.

cards.summary_basic: Fortune (Latin Fortuna) was imagined as a goddess turning a great wheel: as it spins, those at the top (kings, the lucky) are flung to the bottom and the lowly are raised — blind, fickle, and impossible to trust. The Player calls her a 'strumpet' (a prostitute, because she gives her favours to anyone) and prays the gods to 'break all the spokes and fellies from her wheel.'
cards.detail_scholar: The image saturates the play: Hamlet calls himself and others 'Fortune's' playthings; Rosencrantz and Guildenstern banter about living in 'the secret parts of Fortune.' A 'felly' (or felloe) is one of the curved wooden segments of a wheel's rim. Romeo cries 'O, I am fortune's fool!' over Tybalt's body (3.1), and defies 'the stars' (5.1) — the same image of a fickle, ruling Fortune.

cards.title: Alexander and Caesar returned to dust

source.name: Plutarch, Lives (North 1579)
source.citation: Plutarch, Lives, 'Alexander' and 'Caesar' (North's 1579 translation); the memento mori commonplace that the greatest conquerors end as common clay.

cards.summary_basic: Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar were the two supreme conquerors of the ancient world. In the graveyard Hamlet traces their bodies into dust: Alexander's noble dust might end up stopping a beer-barrel's bung-hole, and 'imperious Caesar, dead and turn'd to clay, / Might stop a hole to keep the wind away.' It is the play's bleakest *memento mori* — even the mightiest become mud.
cards.detail_scholar: The 'where are they now?' meditation (the *ubi sunt* topos) and the levelling power of death run from the gravediggers' jokes through 'Alas, poor Yorick' to this passage.

cards.title: Nero, the emperor who killed his mother

source.name: Suetonius; Tacitus
source.citation: Suetonius, Nero §34; Tacitus, Annals 14.1–9 (Nero's murder of his mother Agrippina, 59 CE).

cards.summary_basic: Nero was the Roman emperor notorious above all for murdering his own mother, Agrippina. Going to confront his mother Gertrude, Hamlet warns himself: 'let not ever / The soul of Nero enter this firm bosom' — meaning he will speak daggers to her but must not actually kill her. The allusion measures exactly the line Hamlet refuses to cross.

cards.title: Vulcan's forge and the Cyclopes

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 8.416–453 (Vulcan and the Cyclopes forging armour beneath Etna).

cards.summary_basic: Vulcan was the lame blacksmith-god of the Romans, who forged the gods' armour and weapons in a fiery underground smithy, helped by the one-eyed giants called Cyclopes hammering at his anvil ('stithy'). To say something is 'as foul / As Vulcan's stithy' is to call it soot-black and grimy; the 'Cyclops' hammers' falling on 'Mars's armour' is an image of relentless, crushing blows.

cards.title: Pyramus and Thisbe

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.55-166, in Arthur Golding's English translation (1567).

cards.summary_basic: Pyramus and Thisbe were two young Babylonians whose families forbade their marriage; they whispered through a chink in the wall between their houses and agreed to meet by a mulberry tree outside the city. Thisbe arrived first, fled a bloody-mouthed lion, and dropped her veil; Pyramus, finding the veil and assuming her dead, killed himself; Thisbe returned, found him dying, and killed herself with his sword. The white mulberries were stained dark with their blood — the story the Athenian craftsmen turn into farce at the wedding feast in Act 5.
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid's tale (Met. 4.55-166) was a standard Tudor grammar-school text, read in Latin and in Golding's 1567 English translation, which Shakespeare almost certainly used. The mechanicals' play parodies its high-tragic mode line by line — the alliterative violence ('whereat with blade, with bloody blameful blade'), the mock-blazon, the Wall and the Lion as roles all play comic against Ovid's grave erotic tragedy. Shakespeare returned to the same star-crossed-lovers plot more seriously in Romeo and Juliet, composed in the same years as Dream (c. 1594-96).

cards.title: Theseus (Plutarch's Life)

source.name: Plutarch, Lives (North 1579)
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Theseus, in Sir Thomas North's English translation, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans (1579).

cards.summary_basic: Theseus was the legendary founder-king of Athens — slayer of the Minotaur in Crete, rescuer of Athenian children from the labyrinth, and the captor and reluctant husband of the Amazon queen Hippolyta. North's English Plutarch (1579) was Shakespeare's source for the play's Athenian setting and for Oberon's list of Theseus's earlier loves (Perigenia, Aegle, Ariadne, Antiopa) at 2.1.
cards.detail_scholar: Plutarch's Life of Theseus opens the Parallel Lives, paired with Romulus, and gave Renaissance readers a Theseus who was both heroic founder and notorious philanderer. Shakespeare's Theseus is the courtly lawgiver rather than the unfaithful one — but Oberon's enumeration of his earlier loves nods to the darker side of the tradition. North's Plutarch is the same translation Shakespeare draws on for Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra, and Coriolanus; it was the great Tudor secular history book and the standard source for the ancient world on the Elizabethan stage.

cards.title: Triple Hecate

source.name: Hesiod, Theogony; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 411-452 (Hecate's three domains); Ovid, Metamorphoses 7.94-99 and 7.218-219 (Medea invokes Hecate, the dragon-team of the moon-chariot).

cards.summary_basic: Hecate in Greek religion was a goddess of crossroads and the night, often described as 'triple' because she was identified with one goddess in three realms: Cynthia or Phoebe as the moon in the sky, Diana as huntress on the earth, and Hecate as the goddess of magic and the dead in the underworld. When Puck speaks of running 'by the triple Hecate's team' at the end of A Midsummer Night's Dream, he means the dragons that drew the moon-chariot across the night sky.
cards.detail_scholar: Renaissance mythographers like Natale Conti and Vincenzo Cartari systematised the triple-Hecate identification long before Shakespeare. The moon is Dream's controlling deity — Theseus warns Hermia she may 'live a barren sister' under Diana's altar; the marriage waits on the new moon; the fairy world runs by lunar time. The chthonic, magic-working aspect of Hecate is the one invoked by Macbeth's witches and named in Lear's 'mysteries of Hecat'; here in Dream the lunar and the chase aspects dominate, with the underworld kept lightly in reserve.

cards.title: Cupid's golden and leaden arrows

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.468-474 (two arrows: gold to provoke love, lead to repel it; Apollo struck with gold, Daphne with lead).

cards.summary_basic: In Ovid's Metamorphoses Cupid carried two kinds of arrow: a gold-tipped one that kindled love in the heart it struck, and a lead-tipped one that drove love away. The Apollo and Daphne story turns on this: Cupid shot Apollo with gold and Daphne with lead, so Apollo's pursuit of her was doomed from the start. When Hermia swears 'by Cupid's strongest bow, / By his best arrow with the golden head' (1.1), she invokes the love-kindling arrow as the surest oath she can take.
cards.detail_scholar: The two-arrow motif is one of the most-quoted bits of Ovidian erotic mythology in Renaissance verse — Sidney, Spenser, and Marlowe all reuse it. It explains the asymmetry that haunts classical and Renaissance love-poetry: someone struck with gold pursues someone struck with lead. The motif silently structures the lovers' plot in Dream — the love-juice on the Athenians' eyes works like the golden arrow, kindling new affection; Oberon's antidote works like lead.

cards.title: Philomela

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 6.412-674 (rape of Philomela by Tereus, the sisters' revenge, and the metamorphoses into nightingale and swallow).

cards.summary_basic: Philomela was an Athenian princess raped by her sister Procne's husband, the Thracian king Tereus, who then cut out her tongue so she could not speak the truth; Philomela wove what had happened into a tapestry. The sisters' revenge — feeding Tereus his own son at a banquet — drove all three into the gods' mercy: Philomela became the nightingale, whose mournful song was heard as her voice still grieving. By Shakespeare's day 'Philomel' was simply a poetic name for the nightingale.
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid's Philomela (Met. 6.412-674) is the dark mirror of Pyramus and Thisbe in the same book — both stories meditate on speech, silence, and revenge. In Dream 2.2 the fairies invoke 'Philomel, with melody' to sing Titania asleep; the audience hears the nightingale's mournful classical pedigree under the apparently innocent lyric. Shakespeare uses Philomela far more brutally in Titus Andronicus, where Lavinia, raped and mutilated by sons of Tamora, points to a copy of Ovid's tale to identify her attackers.

cards.title: The Colossus of Rhodes

source.name: Pliny, Natural History
source.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 34.18 (the bronze Colossus of Rhodes).

cards.summary_basic: The Colossus of Rhodes was a giant bronze statue of the sun-god Helios, over a hundred feet tall, that stood at the harbor of Rhodes and counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world. Its name became a byword for anything of overwhelming size.
cards.detail_scholar: Cassius scorns Caesar's outsized power: 'Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus, and we petty men / Walk under his huge legs and peep about / To find ourselves dishonorable graves' (1.2). Pliny describes the bronze Colossus as so vast that few people could clasp its thumb in their arms. The popular picture of the statue straddling the harbor mouth is later legend, but it supplied Cassius his image of ordinary Romans creeping between a giant's feet.

cards.title: Aeneas and Anchises

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 2.707-729 (Aeneas carries his father from the burning city).

cards.summary_basic: As Troy burned, the hero Aeneas escaped by carrying his aged, helpless father Anchises on his shoulders out of the flaming city. The image became the classic emblem of filial duty and of rescue from disaster.
cards.detail_scholar: Cassius belittles Caesar by recalling that he once pulled a drowning Caesar from the Tiber: 'I, as Aeneas, our great ancestor, / Did from the flames of Troy upon his shoulder / The old Anchises bear, so from the waves of Tiber / Did I the tired Caesar' (1.2). The comparison is barbed: Cassius casts himself as the dutiful rescuer and Caesar as the helpless burden, while invoking Aeneas, the legendary Trojan ancestor of Rome. Anchises later guides Aeneas through the underworld in Aeneid 6.

cards.title: Erebus

source.name: Hesiod, Theogony; Virgil, Aeneid
source.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 123 (Erebus born of Chaos); Virgil, Aeneid 6 (the descent to the underworld).

cards.summary_basic: Erebus was the primordial darkness of the underworld, born from Chaos at the beginning of things and used as a name for the gloom souls pass through after death. It stood for the deepest, most absolute darkness imaginable.
cards.detail_scholar: Brutus warns that conspiracy cannot disguise its true face: 'O conspiracy, / Shamest thou to show thy dangerous brow by night, / When evils are most free? ... Hide it in smiles and affability: / For if thou path, thy native semblance on, / Not Erebus itself were dim enough / To hide thee from prevention' (2.1). Hesiod names Erebus among the first beings sprung from Chaos; in Virgil it belongs to the shadowy realm Aeneas enters.

cards.title: Ate, Goddess of Ruin

source.name: Homer, Iliad; Hesiod, Theogony
source.citation: Homer, Iliad 19.91-131 (Zeus deluded by Ate); Hesiod, Theogony 230 (Ate among the children of Strife).

cards.summary_basic: Ate was the goddess of ruin, mischief, and reckless folly who led both gods and mortals into disaster. Her name stood for the blind infatuation that drives people to their own destruction.
cards.detail_scholar: Over Caesar's corpse Antony prophesies civil war: 'And Caesar's spirit, ranging for revenge, / With Ate by his side come hot from hell, / Shall in these confines with a monarch's voice / Cry "Havoc!" and let slip the dogs of war' (3.1). In the Iliad even Zeus is once deluded by Ate and hurls her from Olympus to trouble mankind; Hesiod lists her among the grim children of Strife. To loose Ate is to loose the spirit of ruinous discord.

cards.title: Plutarch's Lives (North's Translation)

source.name: Plutarch, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans
source.citation: Plutarch, The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579).

cards.summary_basic: Plutarch's 'Lives' is a set of paired biographies of famous Greeks and Romans. Sir Thomas North's English translation of 1579 was Shakespeare's main source for his Roman plays, supplying the plots, characters, and many details of 'Julius Caesar.'
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare followed North's Plutarch unusually closely for 'Julius Caesar,' 'Antony and Cleopatra,' and 'Coriolanus,' drawing especially on the Lives of Caesar, Brutus, and Antony. Whole speeches (Antony's funeral oration, the quarrel of Brutus and Cassius) and incidents (the soothsayer, the omens, the proscriptions) come from North, sometimes nearly verbatim. North translated not from the Greek but from Jacques Amyot's French version of 1559; the resulting English prose was itself admired as a masterpiece.

cards.title: Phaethon and the chariot of the sun

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.747-2.400 (Golding's 1567 English translation): Phaethon drives his father's sun-chariot and is destroyed.

cards.summary_basic: Phaethon was the mortal son of the sun-god Phoebus (Apollo). He begged to drive his father's fiery chariot for a single day, but could not control the horses; they scorched the earth until Jove struck him dead with a thunderbolt. Longing for night and Romeo, Juliet cries 'Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds... such a wagoner / As Phaethon would whip you to the west' (3.2) — wishing a reckless driver would race the sun out of the sky.
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid's tale (Met. 1.747-2.400), read in Golding's 1567 English, was a grammar-school staple, and Phaethon became the byword for youthful overreaching that ends in catastrophe — a fitting shadow over Juliet's headlong haste. 'Phoebus' lodging' in the same speech is the sun-god's home in the west, toward which Phaethon would lash the horses. Shakespeare uses Phaethon elsewhere for spectacular falls from height (Richard II 3.3, 3 Henry VI 1.4, Two Gentlemen of Verona 3.1).

cards.title: Diana, virgin goddess of the moon

source.name: Hesiod, Theogony; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 918 (Artemis, daughter of Leto); Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.476-477 and 3.155-252 (Diana the chaste huntress; Actaeon).

cards.summary_basic: Diana (Greek Artemis), goddess of the moon and the hunt, swore never to marry and guarded her chastity fiercely, so her name was Elizabethan shorthand for a cold, unattainable woman. Benvolio says Rosaline 'hath Dian's wit' and stays well-armed 'in strong proof of chastity' (1.1); Romeo, gazing up at Juliet, urges her to 'be not her maid, since she is envious; / Her vestal livery is but sick and green' (2.2) — telling Juliet to quit the moon-goddess's chaste service for love.
cards.detail_scholar: Diana, also called Cynthia or Phoebe, was a favourite flattering type for the unmarried Queen Elizabeth I, so chastity-imagery carried courtly resonance. The play sets Diana's cold moon against Juliet as 'the sun' who should 'kill the envious moon' (2.2). Rosaline's Diana-like vow of chastity is exactly what makes Romeo's early love hopeless and 'Petrarchan' (the cold-mistress convention). Diana is also the huntress whose bath the hunter Actaeon stumbles upon, and one face of the triple moon-goddess.

cards.title: Echo, the nymph who could only repeat

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.356-401 (Golding 1567): Echo, cursed to repeat others' last words, pines away for Narcissus until only her voice remains.

cards.summary_basic: Echo was a mountain nymph punished by the goddess Juno so that she could only repeat the last words she heard. Hopelessly in love with the self-absorbed Narcissus, she wasted away until nothing was left but her repeating voice, haunting caves and hills. Romeo says he would shout Juliet's name until he made hoarse 'the cave where Echo lies' (2.2).
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid pairs Echo with Narcissus (Met. 3): both are studies in love that cannot be returned. The image of a disembodied voice surviving in a cave gave Renaissance poets a favourite conceit. Romeo's hyperbole — that he would out-shout Echo herself — measures how loudly he would proclaim his love if 'bondage' (the fear of being overheard near a hostile house) did not keep his voice down.

cards.title: Helen of Troy

source.name: Homer, Iliad; Ovid, Heroides
source.citation: Homer, Iliad 3; Ovid, Heroides 16-17 (Paris and Helen): the abduction of Helen that began the Trojan War.

cards.summary_basic: Helen, the most beautiful woman in the world and wife of the Greek king Menelaus, ran off with (or was carried off by) the Trojan prince Paris, and that elopement launched the ten-year Trojan War. She was the classical byword for irresistible, ruinous beauty. Mocking the cliches of love-poetry, Mercutio dismisses even 'Helen and Hero' as 'hildings and harlots' beside Romeo's raptures over Rosaline (2.4).
cards.detail_scholar: Helen recurs across the canon as the type of beauty worth a war (compare Marlowe's 'face that launch'd a thousand ships'); Shakespeare anatomises her and the war in Troilus and Cressida. There is a quiet irony in Mercutio's line, since the play's own Paris shares the Trojan prince's name — both are suitors whose desire helps drive a tragedy. 'Hero,' paired with Helen here, is the heroine of the Hero-and-Leander legend (not Helen's companion), another lover famous for a death by misadventure.

cards.title: Rumour and Fame personified

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 4.173-188 (Fama, the swift monster covered in tongues, eyes, and ears); Ovid, Metamorphoses 12.39-63 (the House of Rumour). Englished in Golding's Ovid (1567).

cards.summary_basic: Henry IV Part 2 opens with an Induction spoken by Rumour, a figure 'painted full of tongues,' who boasts of spreading the false report that Hotspur beat the King at Shrewsbury. The image descends from classical poetry: Virgil's Fama (Rumour) in the Aeneid is a swift, monstrous creature covered in eyes, tongues, and ears, flying through the world and mixing truth with lies; Ovid imagines a House of Rumour where every whisper is magnified. Shakespeare turns the figure into the play's presenter and its theme — a realm run on misinformation.
cards.detail_scholar: Virgil describes Fama as growing as she moves, her feet on the ground and her head in the clouds, with as many watchful eyes, loud tongues, and pricked ears as she has feathers (Aeneid 4.173-190); Ovid's House of Rumour stands at the centre of the world, open day and night, where Credulity and rash Error dwell and the smallest murmur swells (Metamorphoses 12.39-63). The Induction's costume — a robe 'painted full of tongues' — was a recognizable emblem from this tradition. By delivering the false news of victory and the true news of defeat in one breath, Rumour frames the whole play's preoccupation with report, reputation, and the gap between word and fact.

cards.title: Astraea

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses; Virgil, Eclogues
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.149-150 (Astraea, the maiden Justice, last of the immortals to leave the wicked earth); Virgil, Eclogue 4.6 ('iam redit et Virgo' — the Virgin returns, heralding a golden age). Englished in Golding's Ovid (1567).

cards.summary_basic: Astraea was the goddess of justice who, in classical myth, lived among humankind in the Golden Age but fled to heaven — becoming the constellation Virgo — when the world grew wicked. Her return became a poetic symbol of a restored golden age. In 1 Henry VI the Dauphin hails Joan la Pucelle as 'Divinest creature, Astraea's daughter' (1.6), casting her as a heaven-sent bringer of a new golden age for France.
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid places Astraea's departure at the end of the Iron Age (Metamorphoses 1.149-150); Virgil's fourth Eclogue made her return ('iam redit et Virgo') the emblem of a coming golden age, a passage later Christians read as a pagan prophecy of Christ. In Elizabethan England the figure carried a sharp contemporary charge: Astraea, the just Virgin, was a favorite symbol of the Virgin Queen Elizabeth I. Charles's application of the image to Joan is therefore double-edged for Shakespeare's audience — a French claim to divine favor that an English crowd, loyal to its own 'Astraea,' would hear with irony, the more so as the play goes on to unmask Joan as a witch.

cards.title: Daedalus and Icarus

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book VIII
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.183-235: the craftsman Daedalus makes wings of feathers and wax to escape Crete; his son Icarus flies too near the sun, the wax melts, and he falls into the sea (the Icarian Sea). Englished in Golding's Ovid (1567). In 3 Henry VI 5.6 the captive Henry casts himself as Daedalus and his murdered son as Icarus.

cards.summary_basic: In the Greek myth, the master-craftsman Daedalus, imprisoned on Crete by King Minos, made wings of feathers and wax so he and his son Icarus could fly to freedom. He warned the boy not to fly too high, but Icarus, exhilarated by flight, soared too near the sun; the wax melted, his wings came apart, and he drowned in the sea below. The tale is the classic image of youthful overreaching destroyed. In 3 Henry VI (5.6), the doomed King Henry likens himself to Daedalus and his murdered son to 'poor Icarus.'
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare knew the tale from Ovid's Metamorphoses (Book VIII), widely read in Arthur Golding's English translation (1567). In 3 Henry VI 5.6 the captive Henry, facing his murderer, turns the myth into an elegy for his son: he is Daedalus and Prince Edward (just butchered at Tewkesbury) is Icarus, while the house of York supplies the cruel Minos who 'denied our course,' the sun that 'sear'd the wings,' and the sea that swallowed the boy. The usual moral of hubris is inverted — Icarus dies not of his own pride but of others' malice. The image of waxen wings and a scorching sun recurs across Shakespeare as a figure for ambition that climbs too high.

cards.title: Juno, queen of the gods

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 1 (Juno, Jupiter's wife and queen of heaven, the enemy of the Trojans); Ovid, Metamorphoses (her jealous vengeance on Jupiter's loves). Greek Hera. In The Tempest 4.1 she presides over the betrothal masque ('Highest Queen of State, Great Juno comes').

cards.summary_basic: Juno was the Roman queen of the gods — wife and sister of Jupiter, king of the gods — and the special protector of marriage and of women. To classical and Renaissance audiences she was the divine guarantor of wedlock, which is why Prospero makes her the chief figure of the betrothal masque that blesses Ferdinand and Miranda, descending to wish them 'Honour, riches, marriage-blessing.'
cards.detail_scholar: Juno (Greek Hera) is queen of the Olympians and goddess of marriage and childbirth; her bird is the peacock ('her peacocks fly amain,' says Iris). In epic she is the proud, jealous enemy of Troy (Aeneid) and the avenger of Jupiter's infidelities (Ovid). The Tempest invokes only her benign aspect as patroness of marriage: her masque enacts a vision of fruitful, chaste wedlock pointedly opposed to the 'bed-rite' Ferdinand has been forbidden before the wedding. Her partnership with Ceres (harvest) joins marriage to fertility and plenty.

cards.title: Ceres and the rape of Proserpina

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses; Ovid, Fasti
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 5.385-571 (Dis carries Proserpina off from Enna; Ceres' grief and search); Ovid, Fasti 4.417-620. Englished in Golding's Ovid (1567). In The Tempest 4.1 Ceres blesses the lovers and recalls 'the means that dusky Dis my daughter got.'

cards.summary_basic: Ceres was the Roman goddess of grain and the harvest (Greek Demeter). Her daughter Proserpina was seized by Dis (Pluto), god of the underworld, to be his queen; Ceres' grief blighted the earth, and the gods decreed Proserpina spend part of each year below and part above — the myth of the seasons. In The Tempest's masque, Ceres blesses Ferdinand and Miranda with 'Earth's increase, foison [abundance] plenty.'
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid tells how Dis, struck by Cupid's arrow, snatched Proserpina as she gathered flowers at Enna in Sicily; Ceres wandered the world with torches seeking her, and in grief made the earth barren until a compromise returned the girl for half the year. In the masque Ceres' first words are wary — she will not come if Venus and her 'blind boy' Cupid are present, 'since they did plot / The means that dusky Dis my daughter got,' blaming Love for her daughter's abduction. The myth makes Ceres the ideal figure to bless a marriage with fertility while guarding it against lawless desire, the masque's central theme. The same myth lies behind Perdita's flower-catalogue in The Winter's Tale ('O Proserpina, / For the flowers now...').

cards.title: Iris, goddess of the rainbow

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 4.693-705 (Iris sent by Juno to release the dying Dido) and 9.803; Ovid, Metamorphoses (Iris as Juno's messenger). In The Tempest 4.1 she opens the masque as Juno's herald, the 'many-colour'd messenger.'

cards.summary_basic: Iris was the goddess of the rainbow and the messenger of the gods — especially of Juno, queen of heaven. The rainbow was imagined as the bright arching road she travelled between heaven and earth. In The Tempest's masque she is the sky-queen's 'watery arch and messenger,' who summons Ceres and the country spirits to bless the lovers on Juno's behalf.
cards.detail_scholar: Iris personifies the rainbow ('thy blue bow,' 'thy saffron wings,' 'each end of thy... bow'); as Juno's herald she is the natural opener of a masque ruled by Juno. Her watery, many-coloured imagery suits the play's element of sea and storm, and her role as go-between mirrors Ariel, Prospero's own airy messenger who in fact 'presents' her. The pairing of rainbow (Iris), harvest (Ceres), and marriage (Juno) builds the masque's promise of a fertile, heaven-blessed union.

cards.title: Dido, queen of Carthage ('widow Dido')

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid, Books 1 and 4
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 1 (Dido, widow of Sychaeus, founds Carthage and receives the shipwrecked Aeneas) and 4 (their love, his departure at the gods' command, and her suicide on the pyre). In The Tempest 2.1 the courtiers wrangle over 'widow Dido' and whether 'Tunis was Carthage.'

cards.summary_basic: Dido was the founder and queen of Carthage in north Africa. A widow — her husband Sychaeus had been murdered — she fell in love with the Trojan hero Aeneas when his ships were wrecked on her shore; when he abandoned her to sail on and found Rome, she killed herself on a burning pyre. In The Tempest 2.1, Gonzalo's claim that Tunis (where Alonso's daughter has just married) stands where ancient Carthage stood sparks the courtiers' mocking quibble about 'widow Dido.'
cards.detail_scholar: Virgil's Dido (Aeneid 1 and 4) is the great epic image of a love wrecked by destiny — the abandoned queen on her pyre. The 2.1 banter ('This Tunis, sir, was Carthage'... 'widow Dido, said you?... widower Aeneas too?') is partly pedantic point-scoring among shipwrecked courtiers, but it quietly seeds the play's themes: sea-voyage and shipwreck, a king's daughter married off to Africa, loss and the hope of return. The shipwreck-on-a-foreign-shore that begins Dido's story is the very situation Shakespeare's castaways are living through. Shakespeare returns to the pair in Antony and Cleopatra ('Dido and her Aeneas').

cards.title: The Harpy

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid, Book 3
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 3.209-269 (the Harpies foul the Trojans' feast on the Strophades; their leader Celaeno prophesies hunger and woe). In The Tempest 3.3 a stage direction has Ariel enter 'like a harpy' and make the banquet vanish.

cards.summary_basic: Harpies were monstrous winged creatures of Greek and Roman myth — birds with the faces of women — who snatched or befouled food and carried off their victims. In Virgil they descend on the Trojans' meal and their leader Celaeno utters a dark prophecy. In The Tempest (3.3) Prospero's spirit Ariel appears 'like a harpy,' claps his wings over a magic banquet so that it vanishes, and denounces the 'three men of sin' for their crimes against Prospero.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare's model is the Aeneid (Book 3): the Harpies foul the feast and Celaeno utters a dark prophecy — exactly the pattern of the 3.3 scene, where the vanishing banquet and Ariel's accusing speech work as a supernatural judgment on Alonso, Antonio, and Sebastian. The harpy's traditional role — to deny food to the guilty and pronounce doom — makes it the perfect disguise for Ariel acting as the instrument of Prospero's (and 'Destiny's') justice. The scene's fusion of spectacle and moral arraignment is among the play's most theatrically striking.

cards.title: Neptune, god of the sea

source.name: Virgil, Aeneid; Homer, Odyssey; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Virgil, Aeneid 1.124-156 (Neptune stills the storm with 'quos ego—'); Homer, Odyssey (Poseidon's pursuit of Odysseus); Ovid, Metamorphoses. Greek Poseidon. Pericles, ruled by the sea, invokes him repeatedly (3.1; 5.1, 'God Neptune's annual feast').

cards.summary_basic: Neptune (Greek Poseidon) was the Roman god of the sea, storms, and earthquakes, and brother of Jupiter. In a play whose hero is shipwrecked again and again, he is the presiding power: Pericles loses his wife to a sea-storm 'on Neptune's billow,' and is finally led to his lost daughter at Mytilene during 'God Neptune's annual feast.' The sea is the play's true antagonist and the instrument of its restorations.
cards.detail_scholar: Neptune embodies the romance's governing force — the sea that wrecks, separates, and miraculously preserves. Classical epic gave Shakespeare both the destructive Neptune and the calming Neptune of Aeneid 1 ('quos ego—'); Pericles uses both, as fortune 'varies' the flood from disaster to deliverance. The same god recurs across the late plays and the wider corpus — Prospero's elves chase 'the ebbing Neptune' on the sands (The Tempest 5.1), and Hamlet swears by 'Neptune's salt wash' (3.2) — so the card serves wherever the sea is personified.

cards.title: Lucina, goddess of childbirth

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses; the Roman cult of Juno Lucina
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 9.281-323 (Lucina, sent by Juno, prolongs Alcmena's labour at the birth of Hercules); an aspect of Juno (Juno Lucina) and of Diana. In Pericles she is invoked at the birth of Antiochus's daughter (1.1) and of Marina at sea (3.1, 'Lucina, O Divinest patroness... gentle thy deafening, dreadful thunders').

cards.summary_basic: Lucina was the Roman goddess who presided over childbirth — a title shared by Juno and Diana, the 'bringer of light' who brings the baby into the light of day. In Pericles she is invoked twice: Antiochus says his daughter was born when 'Lucina reign'd,' and Pericles prays to her as 'divinest patroness' when his wife Thaisa goes into labour during the sea-storm that seems to kill her.
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid dramatizes Lucina's power in the birth of Hercules, where the goddess, sent by jealous Juno, sits cross-legged with clasped hands to delay Alcmena's delivery (Metamorphoses 9). The figure binds birth to danger — apt for a play in which Marina's birth at sea apparently costs her mother's life and names the child 'born in a tempest.' As a function shared by Juno and Diana, Lucina also quietly threads together Pericles's two presiding goddesses (Juno of marriage, Diana of chastity). The name recurs in Cymbeline and Titus Andronicus.

cards.title: The garden of the Hesperides

source.name: Hesiod, Theogony; Apollodorus, Library; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 215-216 (the Hesperides beyond the Ocean); Apollodorus, Library 2.5.11 (the golden apples guarded by the dragon Ladon — Hercules' eleventh labour). In Pericles 1.1 Antiochus calls his daughter 'this fair Hesperides, With golden fruit, but dangerous to be touch'd.'

cards.summary_basic: In Greek myth the Hesperides were nymphs who, with the ever-watchful dragon Ladon, guarded a garden of golden apples at the world's western edge; fetching the apples was one of the labours of Hercules. To call a woman 'this fair Hesperides, With golden fruit, but dangerous to be touch'd' (as Antiochus does of his daughter, Pericles 1.1) is to make her a deadly prize — beautiful, but guarded by death.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare, like many contemporaries, uses 'Hesperides' loosely for the garden itself rather than its nymphs. The image is darkly fitting in Antiochus's mouth: the 'golden fruit' is his daughter, the guarding 'death-like dragons' are the executed suitors who failed his riddle, and the incest he conceals makes the fruit literally forbidden. The same golden-apples image surfaces in Love's Labour's Lost (4.3, 'climbing trees in the Hesperides').

cards.title: Jupiter, king of the gods

source.name: Roman religion; Ovid, Metamorphoses; Virgil, Aeneid
source.citation: Jupiter (Greek Zeus), supreme Roman god of sky and thunder, whose emblem is the eagle. In Cymbeline 5.4 he 'descends in thunder and lightning, sitting upon an eagle' to answer the Leonati ghosts, declaring 'Whom best I love I cross' and leaving a prophetic tablet on the sleeping Posthumus. Cf. Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.166-252 (Jove's justice on mankind); Virgil, Aeneid 1.254-296 (Jupiter foretells Rome's destiny).

cards.summary_basic: Jupiter (Greek Zeus) was the supreme Roman god — ruler of the sky, the thunderbolt, and the other gods — and his bird was the eagle. In Cymbeline he descends on an eagle amid thunder during Posthumus's prison-sleep, silences the complaining ghosts of Posthumus's dead family, and promises that the hero's sufferings are a sign of favour, not anger: 'Whom best I love I cross; to make my gift, / The more delay'd, delighted.' The riddling tablet he leaves is fulfilled by the play's happy ending.
cards.detail_scholar: A theophany — a god appearing in person, here lowered by stage machinery onto an eagle — was an old device of classical and medieval drama; some critics once doubted the scene was Shakespeare's, but it crowns the romance's design, making the gods the visible guarantors of a providence that turns loss to joy. Jupiter's consolation ('The more delay'd, delighted') restates the idea that suffering is a discipline of love. His eagle is at once the king of birds and the standard of Rome, tying the divine plot to the play's British-Roman war: the Soothsayer later reads the Roman eagle winging westward and vanishing in sunbeams as an omen of the peace that ends the play (5.5). Jove is invoked across the canon as the type of supreme, thundering power.

cards.title: Tarquin and the rape of Lucrece

source.name: Livy, History of Rome; Ovid, Fasti
source.citation: Livy 1.57-59 and Ovid, Fasti 2.685-852: Sextus Tarquinius, son of Rome's last king, rapes the chaste wife Lucretia (Lucrece), who kills herself rather than live dishonoured; the outrage drives the Tarquins out and founds the Roman Republic. Iachimo, stealing from a trunk to the bed of the sleeping Imogen, names the parallel: 'Our Tarquin thus / Did softly press the rushes ere he waken'd / The chastity he wounded' (Cymbeline 2.2).

cards.summary_basic: Sextus Tarquinius, son of Rome's last king, raped the virtuous wife Lucretia ('Lucrece'), who killed herself rather than live dishonoured; the scandal overthrew the monarchy and founded the Roman Republic. When Iachimo creeps from a trunk to the bed of the sleeping Imogen to gather false 'proof' against her, he compares himself to 'our Tarquin' approaching Lucrece — framing his stealthy violation of her privacy as a kind of rape, though he takes only a bracelet and the sight of a mole.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare had told the story at length in his narrative poem The Rape of Lucrece (1594), drawing on Livy and Ovid's Fasti. Iachimo's allusion is exact and disturbing: like Tarquin he invades a sleeping woman's chamber by night, and the verse colours his theft of evidence as a sexual crime against her honour. The same figure recurs in Macbeth, where the murderer moves 'with Tarquin's ravishing strides' toward the sleeping Duncan (2.1) — violation imagined as a stealthy, predatory approach. (This Tarquin, Sextus, is the son of the tyrant whose expulsion is treated in the card on Tarquin and the first Brutus.)

cards.title: Apollo and the oracle at Delphos

source.name: Greek religion; Robert Greene, Pandosto (1588)
source.citation: Apollo, god of the sun, prophecy, and music, whose most famous oracle spoke at Delphi. In The Winter's Tale Leontes sends Cleomenes and Dion to 'sacred Delphos, to Apollo's temple' (2.1, 3.1); the sealed oracle declares 'Hermione is chaste... and the king shall live without an heir if that which is lost be not found' (3.2). Shakespeare follows his source, Greene's prose romance Pandosto, in treating 'Delphos' as an island (a long-standing confusion of Delphi with Delos, Apollo's birth-isle).

cards.summary_basic: Apollo was the Greek god of the sun, prophecy, and music, and his most famous oracle gave cryptic answers at Delphi. When the jealous Leontes accuses his queen, he sends envoys to 'Apollo's temple' to consult the god; the oracle clears Hermione and warns that 'the king shall live without an heir if that which is lost be not found.' Leontes defies it — and is struck at once by his son's death, a sign of the god's power that begins his long repentance.
cards.detail_scholar: The oracle is the play's hinge of divine justice. Shakespeare takes from Robert Greene's Pandosto (1588) both the consultation of Apollo and the curious geography that makes 'Delphos' an island — a confusion of the mainland oracle at Delphi with Delos, the island sacred to Apollo's birth. The scroll's conditional prophecy ('if that which is lost be not found') programs the play's whole second half: the lost daughter Perdita — whose name means 'the lost one' — must be found before the curse can lift, which is why Hermione's restoration waits sixteen years. Leontes's blasphemy ('There is no truth at all i' the oracle') is the tragic peak from which the romance turns toward grace.

cards.title: Flora, goddess of flowers

source.name: Ovid, Fasti; Roman religion
source.citation: Flora, the Roman goddess of flowers and spring, honoured at the Floralia (Ovid, Fasti 5.183-378, where the nymph Chloris becomes Flora). In The Winter's Tale 4.4 Florizel tells the garlanded Perdita, queen of the sheep-shearing feast, 'no shepherdess, but Flora / Peering in April's front.'

cards.summary_basic: Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and the spring. At the sheep-shearing feast Perdita is dressed and garlanded as the festival's queen, and Florizel compares her to 'Flora / Peering in April's front' — no mere shepherdess but the very spirit of spring. The image suits a scene awash in flowers and renewal, and quietly hints at the royalty hidden beneath her country 'weeds.'
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid's Fasti tells how the nymph Chloris was transformed into Flora, goddess of blossoms, her breath scattering flowers. Perdita's own famous flower-speech — the daffodils, violets, and 'pale primroses that die unmarried' — makes her a presiding deity of the pastoral world, and her gifts of flowers sorted by season weave the play's themes of age, season, and rebirth. Calling her Flora chimes with Proserpina, whom she names in the same speech: both are figures of spring returning out of loss, like Perdita herself.

cards.title: Venus and Adonis

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.519-559, 708-739 (Golding's 1567 English version was Shakespeare's likely source): Venus (Cytherea) loves the beautiful mortal youth Adonis, who is killed by a boar; she turns his blood to the anemone. In The Taming of the Shrew Induction 2 the Lord's servants tempt Sly with a painting of 'Adonis painted by a running brook, / And Cytherea all in sedges hid.'

cards.summary_basic: Venus (here called Cytherea, after her island Cythera), the goddess of love, fell for the beautiful mortal hunter Adonis and tried in vain to keep him from the chase; a wild boar gored him to death, and she turned his blood into a flower. A favourite subject of Renaissance painters — and of Shakespeare's own early poem.
cards.detail_scholar: In the Induction's gallery of seduction-pictures offered to flatter the gulled tinker, Adonis lies 'by a running brook' while 'Cytherea all in sedges hid' spies on him 'as the waving sedges play with wind' — a teasing, voyeuristic image. Shakespeare expanded the myth into his narrative poem Venus and Adonis (1593), reversing Ovid to make the goddess the frustrated wooer of a coy youth. The painting belongs to a set (Adonis, Io, Daphne) all drawn from Ovid's Metamorphoses, a standard Tudor school text in Golding's translation.

cards.title: Daphne and Apollo

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.452-567 (Golding 1567): the god Apollo pursues the nymph Daphne, who prays for rescue and is turned into a laurel tree as he seizes her; he makes the laurel his sacred emblem. In The Taming of the Shrew Induction 2 a servant offers Sly a painting of 'Daphne roaming through a thorny wood, / Scratching her legs that one shall swear she bleeds.'

cards.summary_basic: The nymph Daphne, fleeing the god Apollo's unwanted pursuit, prayed to be saved and was transformed into a laurel tree at the moment he caught her; Apollo took the laurel as his sacred emblem ever after. It is a classic myth of chastity escaping desire — and of desire's loss made permanent.
cards.detail_scholar: The third of the Induction's Ovidian paintings (with Adonis and Io). Shakespeare embellishes Ovid pictorially — Daphne's legs scratched and bleeding in the 'thorny wood,' so that 'sad Apollo' weeps — turning a chase into a painter's pathos. The laurel (Greek daphne) crowned poets and victors thereafter, so the myth doubles as an emblem of poetic fame won out of frustrated love.

cards.title: Prometheus and the Promethean fire

source.name: Hesiod, Theogony; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 507-616 and Works and Days 42-105; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.76-88 (Prometheus shapes man from clay). The Titan Prometheus stole fire from heaven for mankind and was punished by Zeus. In Love's Labour's Lost 4.3 Berowne says women's eyes 'sparkle still the right Promethean fire' — the living spark of all art and learning.

cards.summary_basic: Prometheus was a Titan who stole fire from the gods and gave it to mortals — the spark of life, art, and knowledge — and was savagely punished for it. 'Promethean fire' became a byword for that divine, life-giving spark. In his great speech defending love, Berowne claims women's eyes kindle exactly this fire in the mind, which dry book-study can never light.
cards.detail_scholar: In 4.3 Berowne argues that love, not cold study, is the true 'academe': women's eyes 'are the books, the arts, the academes, / That show, contain, and nourish all the world,' and 'sparkle still the right Promethean fire.' Shakespeare reaches for the same image at the height of Othello (5.2): 'I know not where is that Promethean heat / That can thy light relume,' where it means the irreplaceable spark of life itself, impossible to rekindle once put out. The myth (Hesiod, Ovid) made Prometheus both mankind's benefactor and the type of the over-reacher punished for stealing what belongs to heaven.

cards.title: Plautus and Roman comedy

source.name: Plautus, Menaechmi; Plautus, Amphitruo
source.citation: Plautus, Menaechmi (the comedy of long-separated identical twins) and Amphitruo (the divine double and the locked-out husband), c. 200 BC. The Comedy of Errors adapts the Menaechmi and doubles its single pair of twins by adding the twin servants from the Amphitruo.

cards.summary_basic: The Comedy of Errors is Shakespeare's most classical play, closely modelled on the Roman comedies of Plautus. Its plot of long-separated identical twins comes from Plautus's Menaechmi; Shakespeare heightens the farce by adding a second set of twins — the servants both named Dromio — borrowed from another Plautus play, the Amphitruo, the source too of the locked-out-husband scene.
cards.detail_scholar: Plautus (c. 254-184 BC) wrote boisterous Latin comedies adapted from Greek New Comedy, full of mistaken identity, clever slaves, and farcical reversals; they were standard texts in Tudor grammar schools, so Shakespeare knew the Menaechmi in Latin (William Warner's English version appeared in 1595, just after the play). Doubling the twins multiplies the confusions: there are now four men who can be mistaken, not two. Shakespeare also frames the Roman farce with the romance of Aegeon and Emilia — a separated family lost and found, drawn from the Apollonius of Tyre tradition — giving the slapstick a tender, redemptive ending the originals lack.

cards.title: Circe and her cup

source.name: Homer, Odyssey; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Homer, Odyssey 10.133-574 (the enchantress Circe gives Odysseus's men a drugged cup that turns them into swine); cf. Ovid, Metamorphoses 14.1-74. In The Comedy of Errors 5.1 Antipholus of Ephesus cries 'I think you all have drunk of Circe's cup,' meaning the whole company is bewitched out of its senses.

cards.summary_basic: Circe was a goddess-enchantress who, in Homer's Odyssey, gave Odysseus's sailors a drugged drink that turned them into pigs. 'Circe's cup' became shorthand for any bewitchment that robs people of their right minds. When the exasperated Antipholus of Ephesus says the others have 'drunk of Circe's cup,' he means the whole city has gone mad or been enchanted.
cards.detail_scholar: The allusion caps the play's running joke that Ephesus is a city of sorcery: again and again the baffled characters explain the inexplicable errors as witchcraft, transformation, or demonic possession. Circe's cup — transformation by an enchanted drink — fits a comedy in which men feel they have lost their own identities and been turned into someone, or something, else. The image recurs across the canon as a figure for the senses overthrown by passion or magic.

cards.title: Ovid's Metamorphoses

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses (c. 8 CE); Arthur Golding's English translation, 1567 — the version Shakespeare knew. In Titus Andronicus 4.1 a copy of the book is carried on stage, and the mutilated Lavinia turns its pages to the tale of Philomela to reveal what was done to her.

cards.summary_basic: Ovid's Metamorphoses is a Latin epic stringing together myths of transformation — people changed into trees, birds, stones, and stars. Arthur Golding's 1567 English translation was Shakespeare's mythological sourcebook, and its stories run all through his work. In Titus Andronicus the book is literally a stage property: the tongueless, handless Lavinia turns its pages to the story of Philomela's rape to name her own attackers.
cards.detail_scholar: More than any other classical text, the Metamorphoses shaped Shakespeare's imagination — Pyramus and Thisbe, Venus and Adonis, Philomela, Actaeon, Arachne, the Golden Age, Pygmalion, and the four ages of the world all derive from it. Titus is his most thoroughly Ovidian play: the rape and silencing of Lavinia rewrites Tereus and Philomela (Met. 6.412-674), and Titus's revenge banquet rewrites Procne's feeding of Itys to Tereus. The same source-bank feeds the narrative poems Venus and Adonis and (with Ovid's Fasti) The Rape of Lucrece. Golding's archaic 'fourteener' couplets are the texture beneath much of Shakespeare's mythology.

cards.title: Cleopatra as the goddess Isis

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony; On Isis and Osiris
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 54 (Cleopatra giving audience robed as Isis); Plutarch, Moralia, 'On Isis and Osiris'.

cards.summary_basic: Isis was the great mother-goddess of Egypt — wife of Osiris, giver of life and of the Nile's harvest, and protector of the dead. The Ptolemaic queens presented themselves as her living image, and Plutarch records that Cleopatra liked to give audience 'in the habiliments of the goddess Isis.' In the play Caesar reports with disgust that the lovers sat enthroned in gold, 'she / In the habiliments of the goddess Isis / That day appear'd' (3.6) — to Rome, proof of their god-king pretensions.
cards.detail_scholar: Isis was worshipped across the Mediterranean, and her cult reached Rome itself, where it was periodically suppressed as a foreign 'oriental' religion. By appearing as Isis, Cleopatra claimed divine queenship and cast Antony as her Osiris (a role Antony also played as the god Dionysus/Bacchus). The identification sharpens the play's contrast between fertile, theatrical, goddess-ruled Egypt and austere, masculine Rome, and it colours Cleopatra's suicide, when she robes and crowns herself once more as the divine queen.

cards.title: The barge on the Cydnus

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Antony (North 1579)
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Antony 26, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579) — Cleopatra's arrival to meet Antony at Tarsus on the river Cydnus, 41 BCE.

cards.summary_basic: In 41 BCE Cleopatra sailed up the river Cydnus to meet Antony at Tarsus in a gilded barge with purple sails and silver oars, dressed as Venus and fanned by boys like Cupids — a calculated piece of theatre that captivated him. Enobarbus's set-piece, 'The barge she sat in, like a burnish'd throne / Burn'd on the water' (2.2), follows North's translation of Plutarch almost word for word.
cards.detail_scholar: North's prose runs: 'she disdained to set forward otherwise but to take her barge in the river of Cydnus, the poop whereof was of gold, the sails of purple, and the oars of silver...' Shakespeare versifies the passage with remarkable fidelity — one of the clearest windows onto his method with a source. It is also dramatically placed: spoken by the hard-headed Enobarbus to skeptical Romans, the description makes Cleopatra's hold over Antony comprehensible to the very men who deride it, and ends 'Age cannot wither her, nor custom stale / Her infinite variety.'

cards.title: Hero and Leander

source.name: Ovid, Heroides; Musaeus; Marlowe, Hero and Leander (1598)
source.citation: Ovid, Heroides 18-19 (the lovers' paired letters); Musaeus, Hero and Leander (late antiquity); Christopher Marlowe's unfinished English epyllion Hero and Leander, completed by George Chapman and printed 1598. In Much Ado About Nothing 5.2 Benedick names 'Leander the good swimmer.'

cards.summary_basic: Leander was a youth of Abydos who loved Hero, a priestess of Venus across the narrow strait of the Hellespont, and swam to her each night guided by a lamp she set in her tower. One stormy night the wind blew out the lamp; Leander drowned, and Hero, finding his body, threw herself from the tower to die with him. They were a byword for passionate, doomed love. Benedick lists 'Leander the good swimmer' among love's famous martyrs (5.2).
cards.detail_scholar: The story was hugely popular in Shakespeare's day through Christopher Marlowe's sensuous Hero and Leander (printed 1598, the years of Much Ado), itself drawing on Ovid's Heroides and the Greek poem ascribed to Musaeus. Shakespeare invokes the pair lightly and often, usually deflating high romance: Benedick mocks the 'quondam carpet-mongers' of love while struggling to write his own verse; Rosalind in As You Like It jokes that Leander 'would have lived many a fair year' but for a cramp on 'a hot midsummer night,' insisting 'men have died from time to time, and worms have eaten them, but not for love.' The Hellespont (the modern Dardanelles) is the strait Lord Byron later swam in homage.

cards.title: Arion and the dolphin

source.name: Herodotus, Histories; Ovid, Fasti
source.citation: Herodotus, Histories 1.23-24 (Arion, robbed and thrown overboard by sailors, is carried safe to shore on a dolphin's back, charmed by his song); Ovid, Fasti 2.79-118. In Twelfth Night 1.2 the Captain tells Viola he saw her brother bind himself to a mast 'like Arion on the dolphin's back' and hold 'acquaintance with the waves.'

cards.summary_basic: Arion was a famous Greek singer and lyre-player who, sailing home rich with prizes, was robbed by the ship's crew and forced to leap into the sea. A dolphin, enchanted by his last song, bore him safely to land on its back. The story stood for the saving power of art and for miraculous rescue from drowning. The Captain uses it to give the shipwrecked Viola hope that her brother Sebastian also survived (1.2).
cards.detail_scholar: Herodotus tells the tale of Arion of Methymna at the court of Periander of Corinth; the dolphin charmed by music became a favourite emblem of poetry's power. The allusion is precisely placed: in a play that opens on the 'food of love' (music) and turns on a sea that seems to swallow a twin, Arion's musical rescue plants the possibility of Sebastian's survival in the first minutes, and ties the comedy's machinery of loss-and-recovery to the redeeming power of art.

cards.title: Elysium

source.name: Homer, Odyssey; Virgil, Aeneid
source.citation: Homer, Odyssey 4.561-569 (the Elysian plain, where chosen heroes live at ease); Virgil, Aeneid 6.637-678 (Elysium, the blessed fields of the underworld). In Twelfth Night 1.2, told the coast is Illyria, the grieving Viola answers, 'And what should I do in Illyria? My brother he is in Elysium.'

cards.summary_basic: Elysium (the Elysian Fields) was the classical paradise, a region of the afterlife reserved for heroes and the virtuous, where the blessed dwelt in eternal ease and sunshine, far from the gloom of the ordinary dead. To say a person is 'in Elysium' is to call them happily dead, among the blessed. Viola, believing her twin drowned, sets the bliss of his Elysium against the strange shore of Illyria in a near-pun on the two names.
cards.detail_scholar: Homer places Elysium at the world's western edge, where there is no snow or storm; Virgil locates it within the underworld as the home of the pious. Viola's pairing of 'Illyria' and 'Elysium' (1.2) is a deliberate, sound-matched contrast that hangs the whole play between death and revival: the brother she mourns as 'in Elysium' is in fact alive in Illyria, and the comedy's work is to turn the elegy into reunion.

cards.title: Pythagoras and the transmigration of souls

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567)
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 15.60-478 (Pythagoras expounds the transmigration of souls — that a soul passes from body to body, even into animals — Englished in Golding 1567). In Twelfth Night 4.2 the disguised Feste quizzes the caged Malvolio: 'What is the opinion of Pythagoras concerning wild fowl?'

cards.summary_basic: The Greek philosopher Pythagoras (6th century BCE) was famous for teaching metempsychosis: that the soul does not die with the body but passes into another, including the bodies of animals, so one ought not to eat meat. Feste, disguised as the curate 'Sir Topas,' uses the doctrine to torment Malvolio, who must deny it (that 'the soul of our grandam might haply inhabit a bird') to be judged sane and freed.
cards.detail_scholar: Shakespeare knew the idea chiefly from the long speech Ovid gives Pythagoras in Metamorphoses 15. The test is a cruel theological joke: 'Sir Topas' demands that Malvolio affirm orthodox Christian doctrine (the soul does NOT pass into beasts) and 'fear to kill a woodcock' (a proverbially brainless bird) before he will grant him his wits. Shakespeare uses the same notion darkly in The Merchant of Venice 4.1, where Gratiano tells Shylock his 'currish spirit / Govern'd a wolf' in a former life.

cards.title: Ganymede, cupbearer of Jove

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567); Virgil, Aeneid
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.155-161 (Jove, in the form of an eagle, carries off the beautiful Trojan boy Ganymede to be cupbearer of the gods); Virgil, Aeneid 1.28 and 5.252-257. Englished in Golding's Ovid (1567). In As You Like It the banished Rosalind takes 'Ganymede' as her male disguise-name (1.3) and woos Orlando in it.

cards.summary_basic: Ganymede was a beautiful Trojan youth whom Jove (Jupiter) carried up to Olympus to serve as cupbearer to the gods — and, in the myth, as the king of the gods' boy-beloved. The name became a byword for a lovely boy, and in its Latin form ('catamite') for a male lover. Rosalind's choice of 'Ganymede' for her disguise loads her cross-dressed wooing with same-sex resonance: a boy actor plays a girl who plays a boy named for Jove's boy-love, courted by a man who thinks 'he' is a youth.
cards.detail_scholar: On the Elizabethan stage every woman was played by a boy, so 'Ganymede' is triply charged — and the play presses the point in Rosalind's Epilogue, spoken in role: 'If I were a woman I would kiss as many of you as had beards that pleased me.' Marlowe's Dido, Queen of Carthage opens with Jupiter 'dandling Ganymede upon his knee,' so the name's erotic colour was current. Shakespeare returns to the playful eroticism of disguise in Twelfth Night (Viola as 'Cesario'), but only here names the disguise for the most famous boy-beloved of myth.

cards.title: Hymen, god of marriage

source.name: Catullus, Carmina; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Catullus 61-62 (the Roman wedding hymns, with the refrain 'Io Hymen Hymenaee'); Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.1-7 (Hymen, summoned to the wedding of Orpheus and Eurydice). In As You Like It 5.4 'a person representing Hymen' enters to present Rosalind and join the four couples, singing 'Wedding is great Juno's crown.'

cards.summary_basic: Hymen (Greek Hymenaios) was the youthful god of weddings, invoked by name in the ancient marriage-song and pictured carrying a bridal torch. By bringing Hymen on stage to close the comedy, Shakespeare crowns the day's tangle of disguise and courtship with the very god of marriage, who sorts out the confusions and blesses four unions at once: 'Then is there mirth in heaven, / When earthly things made even / Atone together.'
cards.detail_scholar: Hymen is a staged masque-figure rather than a 'real' deity in the play's world — a theatrical flourish, like Juno presiding over the betrothal masque in The Tempest, that lets the comedy resolve with ceremony and wonder. The wedding-cry 'Io Hymen' runs through Catullus's marriage-poems; Ovid's Hymen, summoned to Orpheus's wedding, comes with an ill-omened smoking torch, a darker shadow the festive As You Like It sets aside. The figure binds the four marriages into a single rite and turns the disguise-plot's unmasking into a sacrament.

cards.title: The Golden Age

source.name: Ovid, Metamorphoses (Golding 1567); Hesiod, Works and Days
source.citation: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.89-112 (the Golden Age — aurea aetas — when the earth gave all things freely, without law, labour, money, or war); Hesiod, Works and Days 109-126 (the golden race of men). Englished in Golding's Ovid (1567). In As You Like It 1.1 Duke Senior and his men in Arden 'fleet the time carelessly, as they did in the golden world.'

cards.summary_basic: Classical myth imagined human history as a decline from a first Golden Age — a lost paradise of endless spring where the unploughed earth yielded food of itself and people lived without law, property, toil, or war — down through silver and bronze to the present hard 'iron age.' The free forest life of Duke Senior's exiled band, who 'fleet the time carelessly... as they did in the golden world,' is a deliberate return to that ideal of innocent plenty.
cards.detail_scholar: Ovid's four-ages myth (Met. 1) is the fountainhead of Renaissance 'soft primitivism' — the dream of a simple, lawless, propertyless happiness that pastoral keeps alive. The same fantasy shapes Gonzalo's ideal commonwealth in The Tempest 2.1 ('no kind of traffic... no occupation; all men idle'), drawn from Montaigne's essay 'Of the Cannibals.' As You Like It both indulges and tests the golden-world fantasy: the foresters feast and sing, but they also feel the 'icy fang' of winter and kill the deer whose forest they have usurped.

cards.title: Proteus, the shape-changing sea-god

source.name: Homer, Odyssey; Virgil, Georgics; Ovid, Metamorphoses
source.citation: Homer, Odyssey 4.351-570 (Proteus, the Old Man of the Sea, who twists into shape after shape to escape questioners and yields the truth only to whoever holds him fast); Virgil, Georgics 4.387-414; Ovid, Metamorphoses 8.730-737. In The Two Gentlemen of Verona the inconstant gentleman is pointedly named Proteus.

cards.summary_basic: Proteus was a sea-god who could foretell the future but would change into shape after shape — lion, serpent, water, fire — to avoid answering, surrendering the truth only to whoever could grip him fast. His name became a byword for changeableness and slipperiness. Shakespeare names his faithless gentleman 'Proteus,' so the character's very name warns that he will not hold one shape — or keep one love.
cards.detail_scholar: The myth (Homer, Odyssey 4; Virgil, Georgics 4) made 'Protean' a synonym for the shifting and unreliable. The naming is one of Shakespeare's clearest uses of a classical name as a character-emblem: Proteus betrays friend (Valentine) and beloved (Julia) alike, changing shape with circumstance, while the constant Valentine ('strong,' from Latin valens) and the faithful Julia keep their form. The contrast of the steadfast and the Protean runs through the play's debate of love against friendship.

cards.title: The miles gloriosus (the braggart soldier)

source.name: Plautus, Miles Gloriosus
source.citation: Plautus, Miles Gloriosus ('The Braggart Soldier'), c. 205 BC — the Roman comedy whose vainglorious, cowardly captain Pyrgopolynices gave the stock type its name. The type passed through Terence's swaggerer Thraso (Eunuchus) and the Capitano of the Italian commedia dell'arte to the Elizabethan stage.

cards.summary_basic: Parolles is a version of the 'miles gloriosus' — the boastful, cowardly soldier of classical comedy, all swagger, fine clothes, and invented exploits, who is publicly exposed as a fraud. The type is named for the strutting captain of Plautus's comedy. Shakespeare gives the figure several faces: Parolles here, Pistol, Falstaff's wartime bluster, and the fantastical Don Armado of Love's Labour's Lost. The drum-plot, in which the blindfolded Parolles betrays everything to save his skin, is the type's classic unmasking.
cards.detail_scholar: The braggart soldier — empty valour, gorgeous dress, tall tales of battles never fought, cowardice revealed under pressure — was a fixture of Roman New Comedy and of the commedia's Capitano, and was well known to a grammar-school-educated playwright. Parolles ('words,' from French paroles) is the type distilled to pure verbal inflation: his courage, like his name, is only talk. Yet Shakespeare gives him an inwardness the Roman original lacks. Stripped of his disguise and his honour, Parolles does not simply slink off but turns to the audience to accept himself — 'Simply the thing I am / Shall make me live' — a moment of rueful self-knowledge that complicates the easy laughter at his fall.

cards.title: The Greek and Trojan heroes

source.name: Homer, Iliad
source.citation: Homer, Iliad (esp. the combats and councils of Books 1-9): the Greek general Agamemnon and his brother Menelaus; the runner Achilles; the lumbering Ajax; the wily Ulysses (Odysseus); aged Nestor; Diomedes; against them the Trojans Hector, Paris, Aeneas, and old King Priam. Compare Chapman's English Iliad (1598).

cards.summary_basic: The cast is the roll-call of legendary warriors from Homer's Iliad — but Shakespeare deflates them. Achilles sulks in his tent and has an unarmed Hector murdered; Ajax is a slow-witted bruiser; the leaders' grand strategy talk goes nowhere. Knowing the heroic reputations these names carried — Achilles the greatest fighter, Ulysses the cleverest, Hector the most honourable — lets a reader feel how sourly the play undercuts every one of them.
cards.detail_scholar: Each warrior arrives weighted with epic fame, which the play then punctures: Ulysses preaches cosmic 'degree' yet schemes pettily to lure Achilles back to war; Ajax is gulled by flattery; Achilles is vain and treacherous. The mode is satiric and disillusioned — scholars link it to the turn-of-the-century 'war of the theatres' and to a possible Inns-of-Court audience who would relish the mockery of martial honour. On the Greek side the choric voice of this debunking is Thersites (Homer, Iliad 2.211-277, the one common soldier who dares rail at the chiefs), here a 'deformed and scurrilous' railer who calls the whole war 'wars and lechery.'

cards.title: Achilles, Patroclus, and the wrath of Achilles

source.name: Homer, Iliad
source.citation: Homer, Iliad 1 and 9 (Achilles, in anger, withdraws from the fighting and will not be moved) and 16-18 (the death of his companion Patroclus finally drives him back to the field to kill Hector). Compare Chapman's Iliad (1598).

cards.summary_basic: Homer's whole Iliad turns on 'the wrath of Achilles': the greatest Greek warrior sulks in his tent and refuses to fight, and only the killing of his beloved companion Patroclus brings him roaring back to slay Hector. Shakespeare keeps the withdrawal but makes it petty and spiteful, and has Achilles butcher an unarmed Hector by setting his men on him — turning the epic's tragic hero into a vainglorious thug.
cards.detail_scholar: The poem opens by naming its subject, the menis ('wrath') of Achilles. Shakespeare's play foregrounds the intimacy of Achilles and Patroclus that the Iliad leaves more implicit: the camp gossips that Achilles stays abed 'with his masculine whore' (Thersites, 5.1). The ambush-killing of Hector (5.8), ordered while Hector has disarmed, is the play's ugliest deflation of heroic honour. Content-care: Thersites's slurs are the play's nastiest voice, not its endorsement; the nature of the Achilles-Patroclus bond has been debated since antiquity (Plato's Symposium already argues over it), and the note should report that, not settle it.

cards.title: The Judgement of Paris

source.name: Ovid, Heroides; Lucian, Dialogues of the Gods
source.citation: Ovid, Heroides 16.71-88 (Paris recounts the choice); Lucian, Dialogues of the Gods 20. The goddess of strife's golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' set Juno, Pallas (Athena), and Venus to be judged by the Trojan prince Paris, who awarded it to Venus for the bribe of Helen — the act that caused the war.

cards.summary_basic: The Trojan War began with a beauty contest. At a wedding the goddess of strife threw down a golden apple marked 'to the fairest'; Paris, prince of Troy, was made to judge between Juno, Pallas (Athena), and Venus, and chose Venus because she promised him the most beautiful woman alive — Helen, another man's wife. When the Trojans debate whether to keep Helen, this ruinous original bargain lies behind the whole argument.
cards.detail_scholar: The 'apple of discord' and Paris's choice of Venus (love) over Juno (power) and Pallas (wisdom) were a Renaissance commonplace, staged in pageant and painted in emblem. The play's Trojan council (2.2) weighs Helen's 'worth' against the cost of the war: Hector argues by reason that she is not worth one more life, then yields to 'honour' and resolves to keep her — exposing how a single prince's private appetite is dressed up as the public good. The irony deepens the play's anatomy of value: is anything 'worth' what men will pay for it?

cards.title: The Pontic sea (Othello's vow)

source.name: Pliny, Natural History (trans. Philemon Holland, 1601)
source.citation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 2 (the perpetual current of the Pontic sea, which never ebbs back) and Book 6 (the geography of the Pontus, Propontis, and Hellespont), trans. Philemon Holland (London, 1601). Othello 3.3: 'Like to the Pontic sea, / Whose icy current and compulsive course / Ne'er feels retiring ebb...'

cards.summary_basic: Swearing he will never relent from revenge, Othello likens himself to the 'Pontic sea' — the Black Sea — whose cold current was reported to flow only one way, out through the narrows (the Propontis, or Sea of Marmara, and the Hellespont, the Dardanelles) and never to ebb back. The simile makes his 'bloody thoughts' a tide that cannot turn. The detail comes from Pliny's Natural History, widely read in Philemon Holland's English translation of 1601.
cards.detail_scholar: Pliny reports that the Black Sea continually discharges into the Mediterranean through the Bosphorus and Hellespont and never takes a returning tide — an observation Shakespeare converts into a vow: 'Even so my bloody thoughts, with violent pace, / Shall ne'er look back, ne'er ebb to humble love, / Till that a capable and wide revenge / Swallow them up' (3.3). The precise chain of waters (Pontus → Propontis → Hellespont) suggests first-hand acquaintance with Holland's Pliny. The lines appear in the Folio text of the play and add a learned, geographical grandeur to Othello's surrender to Iago's poison, just as the kneeling 'sacred vow' that follows parodies a marriage rite.

cards.title: Timon the misanthrope (Lucian and the man-hater tradition)

source.name: Lucian, Timon, or the Misanthrope; Plutarch, Life of Antony
source.citation: Lucian of Samosata, Timon, or the Misanthrope (2nd c. AD); Plutarch, Life of Antony 70–71 (the Timon digression), trans. North (1579). Timon was already proverbial for misanthropy in antiquity (cf. Aristophanes, Lysistrata 805–20).

cards.summary_basic: Timon of Athens was a byword in antiquity for misanthropy — hatred of all mankind. Lucian's satirical dialogue 'Timon, or the Misanthrope' is the play's key source: there the ruined Timon, deserted by his flatterers, digs in the fields, turns up a hoard of gold, and uses it to torment the false friends who come crawling back — exactly the turn the play takes in Acts 4–5. Plutarch's Life of Antony adds Timon's friendship with the equally biting Apemantus and his epitaph cursing all who pass his grave.
cards.detail_scholar: Lucian supplies the gold-finding and the bitter reversal — wealth returns to the one man who has learned to despise both it and the world that worships it. Plutarch's Antony (chs. 70–71), which Shakespeare knew in North's translation, supplies the frame: Antony withdrawing to a solitary house he called the 'Timoneum,' Timon's companionship only with Apemantus and Alcibiades, and the two epitaphs on his sea-side tomb (one beginning 'Here lies a wretched corse'). The play, written with Thomas Middleton, also drew on an anonymous academic comedy, Timon (c. 1602). Where the classical Timon was a satiric exemplum of ingratitude punished, Shakespeare makes him a figure of genuine, ruinous disillusion.

cards.title: Alcibiades and ungrateful Athens

source.name: Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades (trans. North, 1579)
source.citation: Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades, trans. Sir Thomas North (1579); for the historical figure, Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War. Alcibiades (c. 450–404 BC), Athenian general, ward of Pericles, associate of Socrates.

cards.summary_basic: Alcibiades was a real Athenian general (c. 450–404 BC) — brilliant, charming, and treacherous by turns — repeatedly honoured and then exiled by Athens, who defected to Sparta and to Persia and more than once led armies against his own city. In the play he is Timon's soldier-friend; banished by the Senate for pleading too hotly for a condemned soldier, he marches on Athens in revenge — a public counterpart to Timon's private rage at the ungrateful city. Shakespeare took the figure from Plutarch's Life.
cards.detail_scholar: Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades (North 1579) gave Shakespeare and Middleton the wronged general who turns his sword on his homeland; historically (in Plutarch and Thucydides) Alcibiades was exiled over the mutilation of the Hermae and the Sicilian expedition, not over a single soldier's pardon — the play invents the immediate cause so that his story mirrors Timon's. Alcibiades's measured, civic anger — he enters Athens to punish only his and Timon's enemies, vowing to 'use the olive with my sword' — is set against Timon's total, self-destroying misanthropy: two answers to the same ingratitude. The pairing is itself Plutarchan, for Plutarch set the Life of Alcibiades beside that of the Roman Coriolanus, another great soldier who attacked his own city.
